subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: isolating in the room and only calling home [Pitfall]
passage: The dinner bell rang at eight in the small-town hostel, and Manjula stayed in her room with the door closed. The mess was too noisy, she told herself, and the girls on her floor laughed loudly in a language she only half followed. So each evening she sat on her bed with her phone and talked to Arnab and the others from her old school, telling the same jokes for an hour. On Sunday the floor went to the temple fair together; Manjula said she had a headache. Her old friends were soon busy with their own lives, and the calls got shorter. By November she knew nobody's parents, no shop where the tea was good, and no one to sit with in the library. The town still felt like a place she was only passing through.

qa.q: What did Manjula do when the dinner bell rang each evening?
qa.a: Manjula stayed in her room with the door closed.

qa.q: Why might Manjula have said she had a headache on Sunday?
qa.a: She may feel shy and out of place among the girls and prefer the comfort of old friends, so she avoids the outing.

qa.q: What small step could help Manjula build local bonds?
qa.a: She could accept one invitation, such as tea with a girl from her floor, since small shared moments build the ties that make a town feel like home.

qa.q: How might the girls on Manjula's floor see her staying in?
qa.a: They may think she is uninterested or unfriendly, though they cannot know how uneasy she feels, so a simple invitation could open things up.

grounding: A teen avoids the mess and other students, spends evenings on the phone with old friends and misses the chance to form local bonds.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: isolating in the room and only calling home [Pitfall]
passage:
Every evening at six, when the hostel dining hall in Barcelona filled with noise, Javier took his tray back to his room. He'd eat on the bed with his laptop open and call Ines, his best friend back in Seville. They'd talk for two hours about people he had known since he was six.
It felt safe. The hall felt loud and full of groups who already knew each other.
In week two, the boys on his floor knocked and asked if he wanted to join five-a-side football on Thursdays. He said maybe next time. In week four, someone from his class started a study group. He saw the message too late.
By the end of the second month, Ines had exams and called less. Javier sat in his room on a Friday night and realised he didn't know the name of anyone on his corridor. The city was still a stranger, and so was everyone in it.

qa.q: What did the boys on Javier's floor invite him to?
Why did Javier take his tray back to his room?
qa.a: The hall felt loud and full of groups, so he felt safer and less awkward alone on the call with Ines.

qa.q: What small step could Javier have taken in week two?
qa.a: Say yes to the Thursday football once, since one shared activity can start local friendships.

qa.q: How might Ines see things once her exams begin?
qa.a: Ines may feel guilty calling less, and perhaps worried that Javier has nobody else in the new city.

grounding: Shows a teen avoiding the dining hall and other students, spending evenings on calls with an old friend, and missing the chance to build local bonds.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: isolating in the room and only calling home [Pitfall]
passage:
In the girls' hostel of the engineering college, the mess bell rang at eight every night, and every night Arohi waited until the rush was over, took two rotis back to her room, and phoned her school friends in Jaipur. They had a group call running most evenings. It was the best part of her day.
Aditi, her roommate, kept inviting her: the Sunday walk to the lake, the dance club auditions, a birthday in Room 12. Arohi always said, “Next time, I have a call.”
By the sixth week, the Jaipur calls got shorter. Her friends had new friends at their own colleges. Some nights the call group went quiet. One evening Arohi went down to the mess and found everyone sitting in groups that had formed in September, laughing about the lake walk. Aditi waved her over, and Arohi sat down, not knowing any of the jokes.

qa.q: Where did Arohi's school friends live?
How might Arohi have felt at the mess in the sixth week?
qa.a: Arohi likely felt left out and awkward, not knowing the jokes from outings she had skipped.

qa.q: What could Arohi try now instead of more calls?
qa.a: Go on the next Sunday lake walk with Aditi, and keep calls home to set times rather than every evening.

qa.q: How might Aditi see Arohi's many "next times"?
qa.a: Aditi may feel a little rejected but still cares, which is why she waved Arohi over.

grounding: Shows a teen avoiding the mess and hostel activities, spending evenings on calls with old friends, and missing the chance to form local bonds.
